title: Jeremiah 9:12–26
context: The unit begins with the prophet’s question about who is wise enough to understand why the land has perished (9:12). The LORD answers (9:13–16): the people forsook his law and followed the Baals, so judgment and scattering will come. The LORD of Armies then calls for the mourning women to raise a lament (9:17–22). In 9:23–24 the LORD says not to glory in wisdom, might, or riches, but in knowing him; Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17 echo this saying. In 9:25–26 the LORD announces punishment on those circumcised only in the flesh, Judah among the nations, for Israel is “uncircumcised in heart.” For the heart-circumcision question, see the existing box at Deuteronomy 10:16 (with Deuteronomy 30:6); no new one is added here.

verses.text: Who is wise enough to understand this? Who is he to whom the mouth of the LORD has spoken, that he may declare it? Why has the land perished and burned up like a wilderness, so that no one passes through?
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks who is wise enough to understand why the land perished, and to whom the LORD has spoken. Arminian readers see an invitation to discernment: the disaster has a cause that the attentive can grasp.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that understanding comes from the LORD’s word, not human wisdom alone. Both traditions read the question as preparing for the LORD’s answer, and they agree that true insight into events requires revelation.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Because they have forsaken my law which I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in my ways,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers that they forsook his law, did not obey his voice, and did not walk in his ways. Arminian readers stress that the land’s ruin is traced to the people’s own disobedience, not to fate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as naming the covenant breach, the people’s rejection of God’s law. Shared ground: both traditions read the cause of judgment as moral and covenantal, a forsaking of the law God had given.

verses.text: but have walked after the stubbornness of their own heart and after the Baals, which their fathers taught them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people walked after the stubbornness of their heart and after the Baals their fathers taught them. Arminian readers note that inherited patterns were embraced, so each generation chose to continue in them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see stubbornness of heart as a recurring theme in Jeremiah, showing the depth of sin. Both traditions read the verse as joining personal stubbornness to inherited idolatry, with neither excusing the people.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says, “Behold, I will feed them, even this people, with wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will feed the people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink. Arminian readers see bitter consequences matching bitter choices, as the people taste the fruit of their rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the images as God’s judicial sentence, the bitterness of judgment on covenant breakers. Shared ground: both traditions read wormwood and poison as vivid figures of suffering that follows forsaking the LORD.

verses.text: I will scatter them also among the nations, whom neither they nor their fathers have known. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will scatter them among unknown nations and send the sword after them. Arminian readers note that exile reverses the gift of the land, which was meant to be held in faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scattering as covenant curse, compare Deuteronomy 28:64 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as fulfilled in the exile, while later passages in Jeremiah also hold out hope of return (compare 29:10–14).

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says, “Consider, and call for the mourning women, that they may come. Send for the skillful women, that they may come.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies calls for the mourning women and skillful women to come. Arminian readers see God summoning a public lament, inviting the people to feel the weight of what is coming upon them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that professional mourners were part of ancient grief customs, and God uses them to dramatize judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the summons as a call to take sorrow seriously, not to look away.

verses.text: Let them make haste and take up a wailing for us, that our eyes may run down with tears and our eyelids gush out with waters.
verses.arminianNotes: The mourners are to hurry and wail for us, so that eyes run with tears. Arminian readers note the word us, which joins God’s word and the people’s grief, as if the LORD himself shares in the mourning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call for tears as a fitting response to judgment, which should break hard hearts. Both traditions read the verse as encouraging honest lament, as sorrow over sin and its consequences has a proper place among God’s people.

verses.text: For a voice of wailing is heard out of Zion, ‘How we are ruined! We are greatly confounded because we have forsaken the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: A voice of wailing from Zion cries that they are ruined, having forsaken the land and lost their dwellings. Arminian readers hear the people’s own confession of loss, as they finally feel what their choices brought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cry as the sound of judgment fulfilled, voiced by those who now experience it. Shared ground: both traditions read the lament as a realistic picture of exile’s shock and shame, reported without softening.

verses.text: Yet hear the LORD’s word, you women. Let your ear receive the word of his mouth. Teach your daughters wailing. Everyone teach her neighbor a lamentation.
verses.arminianNotes: The women are told to hear the LORD’s word and teach their daughters and neighbors lamentation. Arminian readers see grief passed on as a lesson, so that the next generation learns the cost of turning from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even the teaching of lament is commanded by the LORD’s word, ordering grief rightly. Both traditions read the verse as a sober call for communal mourning, taught from one generation and neighbor to the next.

verses.text: For death has come up into our windows. It has entered into our palaces to cut off the children from outside, and the young men from the streets.
verses.arminianNotes: Death has come up through the windows and entered palaces, cutting off children and young men. Arminian readers note the image of death as an intruder that no wall or rank can keep out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing that judgment reaches every level of society, from streets to palaces. Shared ground: both traditions read the image soberly, as grief over the loss of the young in a time of war.

verses.text: Speak, “The LORD says, “ ‘The dead bodies of men will fall as dung on the open field, and as the handful after the harvester. No one will gather them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the dead will fall like dung on the field and like the handful after the harvester, with no one to gather them. Arminian readers see the horror of unburied dead as the fullness of covenant curse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the harvest image turned to judgment, with no gatherer to honor the dead. Both traditions read the verse as stark testimony to the seriousness of judgment, and they treat its imagery soberly, without elaboration.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom. Don’t let the mighty man glory in his might. Don’t let the rich man glory in his riches.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the wise, the mighty, and the rich should not glory in wisdom, might, or riches. Arminian readers see a warning against trusting gifts that God gives, as if they were one’s own security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stripping away every ground of human boasting before God. Shared ground: both traditions read the three warnings as exposing false confidence, and they note that Paul echoes the theme (1 Corinthians 1:31 by reference).

verses.text: But let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am the LORD who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness on the earth, for I delight in these things,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Instead, one should glory in understanding and knowing the LORD, who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness. Arminian readers see an invitation to relationship, knowing God’s character and sharing his delight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD himself as the only proper ground of glory, compare 2 Corinthians 10:17 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as central to Jeremiah’s message: true knowledge of God shows itself in loving kindness, justice, and righteousness.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will punish all those who are circumcised only in their flesh:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will punish all who are circumcised only in their flesh. Arminian readers note that an outward sign without inward faithfulness gives no protection, a call to wholehearted response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as distinguishing the outward sign from the inward reality that God alone gives. Shared ground: both traditions read the warning as aimed at confidence in ritual apart from the heart, without dismissing the sign itself.

verses.text: Egypt, Judah, Edom, the children of Ammon, Moab, and all who have the corners of their hair cut off, who dwell in the wilderness, for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: Judah is listed with Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and desert peoples, for Israel is uncircumcised in heart. Arminian readers see the shock of Judah placed among the nations, and the call of Deuteronomy 10:16 still standing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see heart circumcision as God’s work promised in Deuteronomy 30:6. On how command and promise relate, both traditions point to the existing keyContrast at Deuteronomy 10:16 rather than adding one here, and both read Judah’s privilege as no shelter from judgment.
